name: Esquimalt

facts.text: Esquimalt's Tree Protection Bylaw, 2022, No. 3076 protects any tree 30 cm or more in diameter at breast height (1.4 m). It also protects native Douglas-fir, grand fir and western redcedar once 4 m tall, and arbutus, bigleaf maple, Garry oak, Pacific dogwood and Pacific yew from 4 cm DBH. Trees on steep slopes, wildlife and nest trees, and replacement trees are protected too.
facts.sourceTitle: Tree Protection Bylaw, 2022, No. 3076 (Township of Esquimalt)
facts.excerpt: any tree regardless of species having a DBH of 30 centimetres or more
facts.note: V1: CORRECTED. 'Over 30 cm' is now '30 cm or more', and the species thresholds are now visible and added (Schedule A, 'Protected Tree'). CORRECTED: the old sourceUrl (esquimalt-tree-cutting-permit) now serves the permit application form, so sourceUrl points to the bylaw. The copy linked from the Trees page (file named ..._2023_No._3076.pdf) has identical definitions. GAP CLOSED: steep slopes. Cutting on a slope steeper than 30 percent can require a Qualified Professional's report.

facts.text: In Esquimalt you need a permit to cut, remove or alter a protected tree, even one that is dead, dying or hazardous. The permit form covers removal, pruning and work in the protected root zone, and applications go to trees@esquimalt.ca.
facts.sourceTitle: Trees & Urban Forestry | Township of Esquimalt
facts.excerpt: You will need a permit to cut, remove or alter a protected tree. This includes trees which are dead, dying, or hazardous.
facts.note: V1: CORRECTED. sourceUrl moved to the Trees page because the old URL now returns the application form. The email address and the three permit types come from that form (esquimalt.ca/esquimalt-tree-cutting-permit). REMOVED: 'on building projects the tree permit is handled with the building permit', which neither page confirms. The form asks for an arborist report and a tree management plan on development-related applications.

facts.text: Esquimalt residents may prune overhanging branches under 4 inches (about 10 cm) in diameter from a neighbour's tree, following ISA practice. Larger limbs need a tree cutting permit.
facts.sourceTitle: Trees & Urban Forestry | Township of Esquimalt
facts.excerpt: Residents are within their rights to prune overhanging branches that are less than 4 inches in diameter from neighbouring trees.
facts.note: V1: NEW fact. The bylaw defines 'Prune' as cutting branches over 10 cm in diameter and says it does not include topping.

facts.text: Esquimalt's Natural Environment Development Permit Area (DPA 1) covers new buildings and structures, additions over 10 m² and landscaping, with some exceptions. Township-approved ecological restoration and new permeable paths under 1 m wide are exempt.
facts.excerpt: This Development Permit Area applies to: New buildings and structures … Landscaping (with some exceptions)
facts.note: V1: confirmed. node/277 redirects to esquimalt.ca/business-development/official-community-plan/2015-2018-ocp-review/environmental-areas, which describes the 2018 OCP. Development Services: 250-414-7103.

facts.text: Within Esquimalt's DPA 1, new development is not permitted within 20 m of the high-water mark of the Gorge Waterway, or within 10 m of the high-water mark of the Strait of Juan de Fuca.
facts.excerpt: Within Development Permit Area No 1 – Natural Environment, new development is not permitted: within 20 metres of the high water mark of the Gorge Waterway
facts.note: V1: confirmed. The '7.5 m' conflict is RESOLVED: 7.5 m is a separate natural strip along the Gorge, not the building setback (see es-gorge-natural-strip). The DPA 1 guideline wording is 'New buildings/ structures shall not be located within 20 m'.

facts.text: Esquimalt's DPA 1 guidelines ask that land within 7.5 m of the Gorge Waterway's high-water mark be kept as natural as possible, and restored with native trees and plants where it has been altered.
facts.sourceTitle: DPA No. 1: Natural Environment guidelines (Township of Esquimalt)
facts.excerpt: Land within 7.5m of the high watermark of the Gorge Waterway shall be retained in as natural a state as possible.

facts.text: Esquimalt's DPA 1 guidelines ask designers to avoid disturbing or compacting natural soil, to frame public views rather than block them, to prefer natural topography over blasting or retaining walls, and to aim to meet the Canadian Landscape Standards.
facts.sourceTitle: DPA No. 1: Natural Environment guidelines (Township of Esquimalt)
facts.excerpt: Avoid disturbing, compacting and removing areas of natural soil
facts.note: V1: confirmed. CORRECTED: the old sourceUrl (sites/default/files/2026-01/DPA 1 - Natural Environment.pdf) now returns 404, so it was switched to the guideline PDF at docs/business-development/OCP/DPA/. A newer January 2026 edition may exist; re-check before quoting.

facts.text: Esquimalt's DPA 1 guidelines say new landscaping should be mostly native plants and trees, preferably Coastal Douglas-fir zone species, with 'nature out front' in front yards. Plants should be chosen for site conditions, including wind exposure and sea-spray tolerance.
facts.sourceTitle: DPA No. 1: Natural Environment guidelines (Township of Esquimalt)
facts.excerpt: New landscaping shall consist predominantly of native plant and tree species.
facts.note: V1: NEW fact (guidelines 18.5.3.1 to 18.5.3.3). This partly closes the exposure gap: the guideline names sea spray as a site condition.

facts.text: Esquimalt's Pesticide Use Reduction Bylaw No. 2686 regulates and reduces non-essential (cosmetic) pesticide use on lawns, trees, shrubs and flowers on residential and public property. It applies to landscape professionals and lawn care companies as well as residents. Reduced-risk pesticides on the bylaw's list are allowed, and other use needs a permit as a last resort.
facts.sourceTitle: Important Notice to Home Owners, Tenants, Gardeners and Landscapers regarding the use of Pesticides (Township of Esquimalt)
facts.excerpt: applies to all Esquimalt property owners and residents as well as landscape professionals and lawn care companies that do business within the Township of Esquimalt
facts.note: V1: confirmed. CORRECTED: 'bans' is now 'regulates and reduces', matching the sheet. The sheet dates from 2008-09 (adopted July 2008, enforced from July 14, 2009), and its staff names and contacts are out of date, so do not quote them.

facts.text: Under Esquimalt's Boulevard Maintenance Bylaw No. 2860, changing a boulevard needs a Boulevard Alteration Permit. Boulevard shrubs must be drought tolerant and kept under 0.5 m, rocks and gravel need a permit, grass is kept at 15 cm or less, and noxious or invasive plants are not allowed.
facts.sourceTitle: Boulevard Maintenance Bylaw No. 2860, consolidated July 2019 (Township of Esquimalt)
facts.excerpt: noxious weeds or invasive plants are not permitted
facts.note: V1: confirmed (the URL now uses the www. host). Sources: s.2.1(a), (c), (f) and (j), and the permit conditions (d), (e) and (g). Hedges, rocks or gravel are not allowed next to the roadway, curb or sidewalk.

facts.text: Esquimalt holds some of the harbour's last Garry oak habitat, including the 2.4-acre Matson Conservation Area. Gardens nearby suit native, invasive-free planting.
facts.note: UNVERIFIED: secondary land-trust page, from search snippet. V1 could not open it because hat.bc.ca is not on this session's allowed hosts. es-dpa1-native-planting is an official alternative for the native-planting point.
